claim: AAV-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-eYFP was injected into the lateral SuM of VGluT2-Cre mice to express ChR2 in SuM neurons.
source: To optogenetically stimulate SuM inputs in the DG, channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) was expressed in SuM neurons by injecting a Cre-dependent adeno-associated virus (AAV) encoding ChR2-eYFP (AAV-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-eYFP) into the lateral SuM of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGluT2)-Cre mice (Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Hirai et al., 2022; Tabuchi et al., 2022; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used to express ChR2 in SuM neurons, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The vast majority of ChR2-eYFP-expressing SuM boutons in the DG co-expressed VGluT2 and VIAAT.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Boulland et al., 2009; Soussi et al., 2010; Root et al., 2018; Billwiller et al., 2020; Ajibola et al., 2021), the vast majority of ChR2-eYFP-expressing SuM boutons in the DG co-expressed VGluT2 and vesicular GABA transporter (vesicular inhibitory amino acid transporter, VIAAT) (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C-E and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: 95.2 ± 0.3% of ChR2-eYFP labeled boutons co-expressed both VGluT2 and VIAAT.
source: Both VGluT2 and VIAAT (95.2 ± 0.3%), VGluT2 only (2.7 ± 0.2%), and VIAAT only (0%).
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1E showing the proportion of boutons expressing different combinations of markers.

claim: Both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses exhibited paired-pulse depression.
source: As reported previously (Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Tabuchi et al., 2022), both EPSCs and IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses exhibited paired-pulse depression (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1F and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: PPR was significantly different between EPSCs and IPSCs, with EPSCs being more depressed than IPSCs.
source: Importantly, we found that PPR was significantly different between EPSCs and IPSCs; EPSCs were more depressed than IPSCs (Figure 1G; EPSC: 0.46 ± 0.03, n=8; IPSC: 0.6 ± 0.03, n=8, p<0.01, unpaired t test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of PPR values between EPSCs and IPSCs with quantitative data and significance testing.

claim: Stimulating SuM axons instead of terminals yielded similar PPR results to terminal illumination.
source: To avoid this possibility, we stimulated SuM axons instead of SuM terminals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and obtained similar results to terminal illumination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Experimental data from supplementary figure showing that axon stimulation produces similar results to terminal stimulation.

claim: The amplitudes of the second fiber volley were comparable to that of the first fiber volley in paired-pulse stimulation.
source: We found that the amplitudes of the second fiber volley was comparable to that of the first fiber volley (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that ChR2-expressing SuM fibers were activated to the same extent by paired-pulse light illumination.
evidence: Extracellular recordings of fiber volleys showing no change in amplitude between first and second pulses.

claim: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased the amplitudes of both EPSCs and IPSCs.
source: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2.5 to 1 mM decreased the amplitudes of EPSCs and IPSCs (Figure 1H; EPSC: n=14, p<0.001, paired t test; IPSC: n=15, p<0.001, paired t test).
evidence: Experimental data showing the effect of reduced extracellular calcium on synaptic responses.

claim: IPSCs decreased to a greater extent than EPSCs when extracellular Ca2+ was reduced from 2.5 to 1 mM.
source: Remarkably, IPSCs decreased to a greater extent than EPSCs (Figure 1I; EPSC: 45.1 ± 4.1% of reduction, n=14; IPSC: 58.2 ± 2.7% of reduction, n=15, p<0.01, unpaired t test), suggesting different Ca2+ sensitivities for glutamate and GABA release.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of the reduction in EPSCs vs IPSCs with statistical testing.

claim: ω-conotoxin-GVIA (N-type Ca2+ channel blocker) had no effect on EPSCs or IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses.
source: We found that the application of ω-conotoxin-GVIA (ω-CgTx), an N-type Ca2+ channel blocker, had no effect on EPSCs or IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses (Figure 2A; EPSC: 92.5 ± 13.8% of baseline, n=6, p=0.53, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; IPSC: 101.7 ± 11% of baseline, n=6, p=0.89, paired t test).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing no effect of N-type Ca2+ channel blocker on synaptic transmission.

claim: ω-agatoxin-IVA (P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker) suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent at SuM-GC synapses.
source: In contrast, the application of ω-agatoxin-IVA (ω-Aga-IVA), a P/Q-type Ca2+ channel blocker, suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent at SuM-GC synapses (Figure 2B; EPSC: 23.5 ± 4.6% of baseline, n=5, p<0.001, paired t test; IPSC: 23.9 ± 1.9% of baseline, n=6, p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; EPSC vs IPSC: p=0.92, unpaired t test), suggesting that both glutamate and GABA release rely on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at SuM-GC synapses.
evidence: Pharmacological experiment with statistical analysis showing P/Q-type Ca2+ channels mediate both types of transmission.

claim: DCG-IV inhibited EPSCs (IC50=0.11 μM) to a greater extent than it did IPSCs (IC50=0.27 μM).
source: Notably, DCG-IV inhibited EPSCs (IC50=0.11 μM) to a greater extent than it did IPSCs (IC50=0.27 μM; Figure 2C; two-way ANOVA, F1,51 = 8.1, p<0.01).
evidence: Dose-response data showing differential sensitivity of EPSCs and IPSCs to group II mGluR agonist.

claim: 5 μM baclofen suppressed EPSCs more than IPSCs.
source: Similar results were found with the application of 5 μM GABAB receptor agonist baclofen, which suppressed EPSCs more than IPSCs (Figure 2D; EPSC: 51.6 ± 2.4% inhibition, n=8; IPSC: 38.6 ± 4.3% inhibition, n=8, p<0.05, unpaired t test).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing differential inhibition of EPSCs vs IPSCs by GABAB receptor agonist.

claim: BAPTA-AM suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent.
source: We found that the bath application of BAPTA-AM suppressed both EPSCs and IPSCs to the same extent (EPSC: 63.4 ± 12.2% of baseline, n=7, p<0.01, paired t test; IPSC: 63.4 ± 7.8% of baseline, n=8, p<0.001, paired t test; EPSC vs. IPSC: p=0.96, unpaired t test; Figure 2E).
evidence: Experimental data showing equal effect of fast Ca2+ chelator on both types of transmission.

claim: EGTA-AM suppressed EPSCs but did not affect IPSCs.
source: In contrast, EGTA-AM suppressed EPSCs, whereas it did not affect IPSCs (EPSC: 67.4 ± 7.2% of baseline, n=6, p<0.01, paired t test; IPSC: 93.1 ± 9.2% of baseline, n=6, p=0.40, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; EPSC vs. IPSC: p<0.05, unpaired t test; Figure 2E).
evidence: Experimental data showing differential effect of slow Ca2+ chelator on EPSCs vs IPSCs.

claim: The spatial coupling between Ca2+ channels and synaptic vesicles is tighter for GABA release than for glutamate release.
source: These results indicate tighter coupling between Ca2+ channels and synaptic vesicles for GABA release than for glutamate release.
evidence: Inference drawn from the differential effects of BAPTA-AM and EGTA-AM on EPSCs and IPSCs.

claim: Minimal light stimulation detected 86 EPSC-only, 67 IPSC-only, and 19 biphasic events from 1700 trials across 17 cells.
source: Using this method, we analyzed 1700 trials from 17 cells and detected 86 EPSC-only, 67 IPSC-only, and 19 biphasic events (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Quantitative data from minimal stimulation experiments showing the distribution of response types.

claim: Independent EPSCs and IPSCs are the majority of synaptic responses evoked by minimal stimulation.
source: These results indicate that independent EPSCs and IPSCs are the majority of synaptic responses (Figure 3D; EPSC: 5.1 ± 0.5% probability; IPSC: 3.9 ± 0.4% probability; biphasic: 1.1 ± 0.3% probability, n=17, EPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001; IPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing that independent responses are significantly more common than biphasic responses.

claim: The amplitudes and decay of minimal light stimulation-evoked EPSCs were not changed by application of picrotoxin.
source: We found that the amplitudes and decay of minimal light stimulation-evoked EPSCs were not changed by the application of the GABAA receptor blocker picrotoxin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Pharmacological control experiment showing that EPSCs are not contaminated by GABAergic responses.

claim: The amplitudes and rise time of minimal light stimulation-evoked IPSCs were not altered by application of NBQX.
source: Similarly, the amplitudes and rise time of minimal light stimulation-evoked IPSCs were not altered by application of the AMPA/kainate receptor blocker NBQX (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Pharmacological control experiment showing that IPSCs are not contaminated by glutamatergic responses.

claim: The amplitudes of EPSCs and IPSCs evoked by minimal stimulation were identical to those of strontium-induced asynchronous EPSCs and IPSCs.
source: Furthermore, by comparing minimal stimulation-evoked PSCs with strontium-induced asynchronous PSCs (see below), we found that the amplitudes of EPSCs and IPSCs evoked by minimal stimulation were identical to those of strontium-induced asynchronous EPSCs and IPSCs, respectively (Figure 3G), suggesting that PSCs evoked by minimal stimulation were mediated by a single vesicle release.
evidence: Comparison of amplitude distributions showing that minimal stimulation evokes unitary responses.

claim: The majority of asynchronous synaptic events induced by Sr2+ were EPSC-only or IPSC-only, whereas biphasic PSCs represented only a minor population.
source: By repeating the light stimulation of the SuM inputs 30 times (every 10 s), we found that the majority of asynchronous synaptic events were EPSC-only or IPSC-only, whereas biphasic PSCs represented only a minor population (Figure 3F; EPSC: 27.9 ± 4.7 events; IPSC: 23.4 ± 4.2 events; biphasic: 2.5 ± 0.5 events, n=11, EPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001; IPSC vs biphasic, p<0.001, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of asynchronous release events showing predominance of independent responses.

claim: Almost all VGluT2-positive terminals in the GC layer co-expressed VIAAT.
source: As shown previously (Uchigashima et al., 2011), double immunofluorescence revealed that almost all VGluT2-positive terminals in the GC layer co-expressed VIAAT (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of glutamatergic and GABAergic markers in terminals.

claim: SuM terminals formed asymmetric and symmetric synapses, characteristic of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, respectively.
source: Further post-embedding immunogold EM (Figure 4C and D) showed that these terminals formed asymmetric and symmetric synapses, characteristic of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, respectively (Figure 4C and D), confirming previous observations (Boulland et al., 2009; Soussi et al., 2010; Root et al., 2018; Billwiller et al., 2020).
evidence: Electron microscopy data showing morphological characteristics of synapses formed by SuM terminals.

claim: A single nerve terminal formed both asymmetric and symmetric synapses on a GC soma.
source: Conventional EM using serial ultrathin sections also revealed that a single nerve terminal formed both asymmetric and symmetric synapses on a GC soma (Figure 4E).
evidence: Serial section electron microscopy showing that individual terminals form both synapse types.

claim: Retrograde tracing did not reveal any retrogradely labeled neurons in the VTA after injection into the dorsal DG.
source: However, our retrograde tracing with fluorescent microspheres injected into the dorsal DG did not reveal any retrogradely labeled neurons in the VTA, while labeled neurons were successfully observed in the SuM and entorhinal cortex (EC) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Anatomical tracing experiment showing that VTA does not project to the dorsal DG in the conditions tested.

claim: The majority of VGluT2-positive terminals (52.5%) were associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1.
source: Specifically, the majority of VGluT2-positive terminals were associated with both GluN1 and GABAAα1 (52.5%), and the remainder were associated with GABAAα1 (22.1%) alone or GluN1 (25.4%) alone (Figure 4I).
evidence: Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis showing the distribution of postsynaptic markers at SuM terminals.

claim: The average distance between GluN1 and GABAAα1 clusters adjacent to the same VGluT2-positive terminal was 397.5 ± 8.75 nm.
source: On average, the distance was 397.5 ± 8.75 nm, and most VGluT2-positive terminals (79.2%, 191 out of 241) form glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses within 500 nm (Figure 4J).
evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis of the spatial relationship between glutamatergic and GABAergic postsynaptic sites.

claim: Trains of 10 light stimuli at 5, 10, and 20 Hz elicited pronounced short-term synaptic depression of EPSCs with stronger depression at higher frequencies.
source: We found that trains of 10 light stimuli at 5, 10, and 20 Hz elicited pronounced short-term synaptic depression of EPSCs during train with stronger depression at higher frequencies (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing frequency-dependent depression of glutamatergic transmission.

claim: IPSCs exhibited short-term synaptic depression across all tested frequencies, but GABAergic co-transmission showed a similar magnitude of depression across all frequencies.
source: In marked contrast to EPSCs, while IPSCs also exhibited short-term synaptic depression across all tested frequencies, GABAergic co-transmission showed a similar magnitude of depression across all frequencies (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing frequency-independent depression of GABAergic transmission.

claim: The depression of EPSCs was stronger than that of IPSCs at 10 Hz and 20 Hz.
source: Indeed, comparing the amplitudes of the 10th EPSCs with those of the 10th IPSCs indicated that the depression of EPSCs was stronger than that of IPSCs at 10 Hz and 20 Hz (Figure 5G).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of the magnitude of depression between EPSCs and IPSCs at different frequencies.

claim: 10 Hz train light illumination induced a stronger depression of EPSCs than of IPSCs when recorded simultaneously.
source: We found that 10 Hz train light illumination induced a stronger depression of EPSCs than of IPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), thereby decreasing the EPSC/IPSC ratio during the high-frequency train stimulation.
evidence: Simultaneous recording of EPSCs and IPSCs showing differential depression during train stimulation.

claim: The fiber volley induced by trains of 10 light stimuli was comparable across all tested frequencies.
source: We confirmed that the fiber volley induced by trains of 10 light stimuli was comparable across all tested frequencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that a similar number of SuM fibers were activated with each light pulse during trains.
evidence: Extracellular recordings showing consistent fiber activation across different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Short-term depression of EPSCs with high-frequency light stimulation (10 Hz and 20 Hz) was not affected by γDGG.
source: Under these conditions, short-term depression with high-frequency light stimulation (10 Hz and 20 Hz) was not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment ruling out postsynaptic AMPA receptor saturation/desensitization as the mechanism of depression.

claim: Short-term depression of IPSCs in response to 10 light pulses at 10 Hz and 20 Hz did not differ before and after the application of TPMPA.
source: We found that 300 μM TPMPA reduced the amplitude of IPSCs (47.1 ± 3.8% reduction, n=11, p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), while short-term depression of IPSCs in response to 10 light pulses at 10 Hz and 20 Hz did not differ before and after the application of TPMPA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C, D), excluding the involvement of GABAA receptor saturation in the short-term depression of IPSCs at SuM-GC synapses, suggesting a presynaptic origin of this short-term plasticity.
evidence: Pharmacological experiment ruling out postsynaptic GABAA receptor saturation as the mechanism of depression.

claim: Paired light illumination significantly enhanced GC firing compared to sinusoidal current injections without light stimulation at 5 Hz.
source: Paired light illumination significantly enhanced GC firing compared to sinusoidal current injections without light stimulation throughout the trial (10 stimuli; Figure 6A and D).
evidence: Current-clamp recordings showing that SuM activation enhances granule cell firing at 5 Hz.

claim: The probability of spikes further increased when GABAergic transmission was blocked by picrotoxin at 5 Hz stimulation.
source: Notably, the probability of spikes further increased when GABAergic transmission was blocked by picrotoxin (Figure 6A and D).
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing that GABAergic co-transmission limits the excitatory effect of SuM inputs at 5 Hz.

claim: At higher frequencies (10 Hz and 20 Hz), the enhancement of spike probability by SuM activation was attenuated and disappeared in the last few stimulations.
source: In striking contrast, at higher frequencies (10 Hz and 20 Hz), the enhancement of spike probability by SuM activation was attenuated and disappeared in the last few stimulations (Figure 6B, C, E and F).
evidence: Current-clamp recordings showing frequency-dependent filtering of SuM excitatory effects.

claim: In the presence of picrotoxin, SuM activation by light stimulation enhanced GC firing even in the last few stimulations at 10 Hz and 20 Hz.
source: Importantly, in the presence of picrotoxin, SuM activation by light stimulation enhanced GC firing, even in the last few stimulations (Figure 6B, C, E and F), suggesting that SuM glutamatergic co-transmission still exerted excitatory effects in the later cycle, even during the short-term depression of glutamate release.
evidence: Pharmacological experiment showing that GABAergic co-transmission filters out excitatory effects at high frequencies.

claim: Glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within the SuM terminals.
source: Our findings suggest that glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within the SuM terminals, and reveal that distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
evidence: Summary statement in the abstract integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: Distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
source: Our findings suggest that glutamate and GABA are co-released from different synaptic vesicles within the SuM terminals, and reveal that distinct transmission modes of glutamate/GABA co-release serve as frequency-dependent filters of SuM inputs.
evidence: Summary statement in the abstract integrating the functional implications of the findings.

claim: The co-release of glutamate and GABA has been identified in several brain regions of the adult brain.
source: The co-release of glutamate and GABA, both fast-acting and functionally opposing neurotransmitters, has recently been identified in several brain regions of the adult brain (Trudeau and El Mestikawy, 2018; Kim and Sabatini, 2022; Wallace and Sabatini, 2023).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to review articles on glutamate/GABA co-release.

claim: The lateral habenula neurons receive glutamate/GABA co-releasing synaptic inputs from the entopeduncular nucleus.
source: The lateral habenula neurons receive glutamate/GABA co-releasing synaptic inputs from the entopeduncular nucleus (EP) (Shabel et al., 2014; Wallace et al., 2017; Root et al., 2018) and ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Root et al., 2014; Yoo et al., 2016; Root et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about anatomical connectivity supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) neurons projecting to the DG co-release glutamate and GABA.
source: Hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) neurons projecting to the DG also co-release glutamate and GABA (Pedersen et al., 2017; Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Billwiller et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Ajibola et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about SuM-DG co-release supported by multiple citations.

claim: Electrophysiological studies have demonstrated the co-packaging of glutamate and GABA in the same synaptic vesicles at EP-lateral habenular synapses.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that both glutamate and GABA are co-packaged in the same synaptic vesicles in the lateral habenula (Shabel et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about findings in lateral habenula supported by citations.

claim: An immuno-EM study demonstrated that glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicle populations are segregated in the axon terminals of the EP and VTA projections in the lateral habenula.
source: Conversely, an immunoelectron microscopy (immuno-EM) study demonstrated that glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicle populations are segregated in the axon terminals of the EP and VTA projections in the lateral habenula, and that single terminals form both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Root et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about anatomical findings in lateral habenula supported by citation.

claim: Glutamate and GABA are segregated into distinct vesicle populations within the axon terminals of the SuM projections in the DG.
source: The same study also reported that glutamate and GABA are segregated into distinct vesicle populations within the axon terminals of the SuM projections in the DG (Root et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about anatomical findings in DG supported by citation.

claim: The mode of co-release of glutamate and GABA from the SuM terminals has never been functionally addressed.
source: However, the mode of co-release of glutamate and GABA from the SuM terminals has never been functionally addressed.
evidence: Statement identifying a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Different PPRs between co-transmission of dual-neurotransmitters are found in the retina (acetylcholine and GABA) and striatum (dopamine and glutamate or GABA).
source: Different release properties of dual-neurotransmitter neurons have been reported in other synaptic circuits. Different PPRs (Lee et al., 2010; Silm et al., 2019; Zych and Ford, 2022) and Ca2+-sensitivities (Lee et al., 2010; Zych and Ford, 2022) between co-transmission of dual-neurotransmitters are found in the retina (acetylcholine and GABA) and striatum (dopamine and glutamate or GABA).
evidence: Statement about findings in other brain regions supported by citations.

claim: Different reliance on Ca2+ channels for distinct neurotransmitters have been reported in the retina, striatum, and hippocampus.
source: Different reliance on Ca2+ channels for distinct neurotransmitters have been reported in the retina (acetylcholine and GABA; Lee et al., 2010), striatum (dopamine and glutamate; Silm et al., 2019), and hippocampus (acetylcholine and GABA; Takács et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about findings in other brain regions supported by citations.

claim: Differential release properties of two neurotransmitters indicate a separate release from distinct vesicle pools.
source: These differential release properties of the two neurotransmitters indicate a separate release from distinct vesicle pools (Lee et al., 2010; Takács et al., 2018; Silm et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretive statement about the implications of differential release properties, supported by citations.

claim: The excitatory transmission of SuM-CA2 pyramidal neuron synapses is mediated by P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.
source: Interestingly, the excitatory transmission of SuM-CA2 pyramidal neuron synapses, an exclusive glutamatergic synapse (Chen et al., 2020), is also mediated by P/Q-type Ca2+ channels (Robert et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about findings at a different synapse type supported by citations.

claim: Neurotransmitter release from SuM neurons depends on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, irrespective of the target neurons.
source: Therefore, neurotransmitter release from SuM neurons depends on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, irrespective of the target neurons.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing findings at SuM-GC and SuM-CA2 synapses.

claim: A previous biochemical study detected VGluT2 and VIAAT in distinct purified synaptic vesicles from the hippocampus.
source: A previous biochemical study detected VGluT2 and VIAAT in distinct purified synaptic vesicles from the hippocampus (Boulland et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement about biochemical findings supported by citation.

claim: Differences in transport mechanisms between glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicles have been reported.
source: Moreover, differences in transport mechanisms between glutamatergic and GABAergic vesicles have been reported (Farsi et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about vesicle transport mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: The theta-rhythm in the hippocampus is associated with synchronized SuM activity.
source: The fact that the theta-rhythm in the hippocampus is associated with synchronized SuM activity (Kirk and McNaughton, 1991; Kocsis and Vertes, 1994; Ito et al., 2018; Farrell et al., 2021) has important implications for the low-pass filtering of this synapse.
evidence: Statement about SuM activity patterns supported by citations.

claim: SuM inputs may transfer their train information exclusively at the theta frequency, which could contribute to theta-mediated information processing in SuM-hippocampal circuits.
source: As SuM inputs act as excitatory at 5 Hz (theta) train stimulation, but not at higher frequencies, SuM inputs may transfer their train information exclusively at the theta frequency, which could contribute to theta-mediated information processing in SuM-hippocampal circuits and their relevant brain functions, including cognitive, sleep, and navigation processes (Pedersen et al., 2017; Billwiller et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Farrell et al., 2021; Kesner et al., 2023).
evidence: Speculative statement about functional implications supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Low-pass filtering of SuM inputs could prevent the over-excitation of GCs, leading to anti-seizure effects.
source: In addition to SuM inputs, GCs receive EC inputs as the main excitatory inputs for discharge, and other excitatory inputs from hilar mossy cells (Hashimotodani et al., 2017). Therefore, low-pass filtering of SuM inputs could prevent the over-excitation of GCs, leading to anti-seizure effects.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential functional consequences of the findings.

claim: Long-term potentiation at SuM-GC synapses selectively occurs of glutamatergic co-transmission.
source: In contrast to the presynaptic origin of short-term plasticity at SuM-GC synapses, we previously demonstrated the postsynaptically induced long-term potentiation at SuM-GC synapses, which selectively occurs of glutamatergic co-transmission (Hirai et al., 2022; Tabuchi et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about previous findings from the same group supported by citations.

claim: SuM inputs play diverse roles in modulating GC output via short- and long-term plasticity with pre- and postsynaptic distinct mechanisms.
source: Our findings suggest that SuM inputs play diverse roles in modulating GC output via short- and long-term plasticity with pre- and postsynaptic distinct mechanisms, respectively.
evidence: Summary statement integrating current findings with previous work.

claim: C57BL/6 and VGluT2-Cre mice of either sex aged 6–7 weeks were used for electrophysiological experiments.
source: C57BL/6 and VGluT2-Cre mice (Jackson Labs, Slc17a6tm2(cre)Lowl/J, stock #016963) of either sex aged 6–7 weeks were used for electrophysiological experiments and male C57BL/6 mice at 2–3 months of age were used for anatomical experiments (Figure 4).
evidence: Description of experimental animals used in the study.

claim: 200 nL of AAV1-EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP was injected into the SuM at specific stereotaxic coordinates.
source: 200 nL of AAV1-EF1a-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP (Addgene) was injected into the SuM (relative to bregma, AP: −2.2 mm, ML: ±0.5 mm, DV: −4.85 mm) at a rate of 50 nL/min.
evidence: Description of viral injection procedure with specific parameters.

claim: Acute transverse hippocampal slices (300-μm-thick) were prepared from mice 3–4 weeks after AAV injection.
source: Acute transverse hippocampal slices (300-μm-thick) were prepared from mice 3–4 weeks after AAV injection.
evidence: Description of slice preparation timing and thickness.

claim: Whole-cell recordings were made from GCs using an infrared differential interference contrast microscopy.
source: Whole-cell recordings using an EPC10 (HEKA Electronik) or IPA amplifier (Sutter Instruments) were made from GCs using an infrared differential interference contrast microscopy (IR-DIC, Olympus, BX51WI).
evidence: Description of electrophysiological recording methods.

claim: ChR2-expressing SuM fibers were activated by a pulse of 470 nm blue light (1–5ms duration, 5.0–10.5 mW/mm2).
source: ChR2-expresing SuM fibers were activated at 0.05 Hz by a pulse of 470 nm blue light (1–5ms duration, 5.0–10.5 mW/mm2) delivered through a 40× objective attached to a microscope using an LED (Mightex or ThorLabs).
evidence: Description of optogenetic stimulation parameters.
